course.title: GI bleeding
course.html:
Classification

Amount of blood loss
(prognosis)		a) Small bleeding: < 10% of total blood volume (500 ml), normal TAS and HR
b) Medium bleeding: <20% of blood volume (500-1000 ml), TAS > 100 mmHq, HR <100
beats/min, peripheral vasoconstriction
c) Intense bleedings <30% of circulating volume (1500-2000 ml), TAS <100 mmHq, HR> 120
beats/min lipotemia, tachypnea, oliguria
d) Severe bleeding: loss >50% (2000-3000 ml), TAS <70 mmHq, peripheral filiform pulse
e) Cataclysmic bleeding: rapid and massive blood loss, often fatal
Bleeding site
(topography)		Upper GI bleeding: between oropharynx and duodenal-jejunal angle
Lower GI bleeding: between duodenal-jejunal angle and anus
Rate of bleedingAcute = large amount of blood rapidly lost → significant hemodynamic disturbances
Chronic = small, repeated, usually occult losses → severe anemia

Upper GI bleeding

  • Blood loss between oropharynx (pharyngo-esophageal junction) & duodenal-jejunal angle (Treitz angle)
  • Externalized by
  • Hematemesis
  • Melena
  • Hematochezia

Etiology

Digestive causeEsophagus: esophageal varices, Mallory-Weiss snd, esophagitis, benign/ malignant tumors,
iatrogenic bleeding, trauma by foreign bodies, Boerhaaven syndrome, esophageal diverticula
Gastric or duodenal: gastric or duodenal ulcers, gastritis, malignant/ benign tumors, gastric
polyps, trauma, operations, foreign bodies, Menetrier's syndrome, hiatal hernia, aneurisms,
syphilis or tuberculosis, ampulloma, Crohn's disease
Annexes of GI
tract		- Hepatic and extrahepatic biliary tract trauma, choledochal cancer, iatrogenic causes
- Liver cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari snd, hemangioma, post-traumatic hemobilia, hepatic a. aneurysm
- Acute pancreatitis, pancreatic tumors
Extradigestive
causes		- Blood swallowed: epistaxis, hemoptysis
- Stress ulcer (Cushing ulcers, severe burns (Curling ulcers), toxic-septic shock, surgery)
- Portal hypertension
- Hematological (acute leukemias, hemophilia, pernicious anemia, malignant lymphomas)
- Medically: NSAIDs, steroids, anticoagulants, cytostatic agents, alcohol
  • Most common
Esophageal varicesAlcoholism, hepatitis B, C → liver cirrhosis/ HCC, portal vein thrombosis → PTH →
esophageal varices
Gastric and duodenal ulcer- Hemorrhagic duodenal ulcers usually located on posterior surface
Acute/ chronic gastritisAcute/ chronic gastritis- Often multiple erosions at fundus and body of stomach
- Acute one is frequently hemorrhagic → NSAID’s, alcohol, steroids
- Chronic one is commonly associated with H. pylori
Stress ulcera) Curling ulcer: severe burns
b) Cushing ulcer: intracranial interventions or pathologies
Gastric cancer

Clinical manifestation

  • S. unten Tabelle

Classification

Small GI bleedingBlood loss: < 500ml
BP/ HR: normal		Ht: > 30%
Hb: 10-12 g/dl
Moderate GI bleedingBlood loss: 500-1000ml
sBP > 100 and HR < 100
+ pallor, cold sweating, tachypnea		Ht: 25-30%
Hb: 8-10 g/dl
Large upper GI bleedingBlood loss: 1500-2000ml
sBP <100 and HR > 100-200
+ fainting, cold sweating, tachypnea, oliguria		Ht: < 25 %
Hb: 5-8 g/dl
Severe upper GI bleedingBlood loss: 2000-3000ml
sBP < 70
+ weak or no pulse
Cataclysmic upper GIMassive and rapid bleeding → death in short time
before therapeutic intervention could succeed
bleeding

Diagnosis

  • 1. Clinical exam
  • Anamnesis (diseases, alcohol consumption, drugs)
  • Physical exam (pale, cold, moist skin; cyanosis, tachypnea, tachycardia)
  • Basic life parameters (hypovolemia or shock signs → thirst, dizziness, hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea,

dyspnea, collapse and coma) → BP, HR, O2 sat, ECG

  • Presence of ascites, collateral circulation, palpation of abdominal tumors
  • Digital rectal exam confirms melena or hematochezia
  • 2. Lab
  • Hb, Ht, coagulation
  • Blood group, Rh (cross-matching)
  • Liver function (serum protein, bilirubin, ALP, GGT, GPT)
  • Renal function (urea, crea, electrolytes,)
  • 3. Imaging
  • Upper GI endoscopy
    • Performed after hemodynamic stabilization or in emergency
    • In any patient where bleeding is suspected
    • Can determine bleeding location
    • Therapeutic methods

+ Selective arteriography (can highlight small bleedings)

+ Scintigraphy

+ Angio CT

+ Digestive video capsule (exploration of GI segments which endoscope can’t reach; but no biopsy)

+ Hemoccult test

Positive diagnosis and differential diagnosis

  • Hematemesis – haemoptysis
  • Melena - ingestion of drugs (iron, bismuth, charcoal)
  • Lower gastrointestinal bleeding, swallowed epistaxis, gums bleeding

Prophylaxis

  • Treatment of gastroduodenal ulcers with Helicobacter pylori eradication and systematic administration of PPI
  • Endoscopic treatment of esophageal varices before rupture
  • Early detection of tumors

Treatment

Hemodynamic instable- 2 large i.v. lines or CVC → blood volume restoration
- Crystalloid solutions i.v. (Ringer's or saline), Blood transfusion
- O2 administration
- Nasogastric tube (diagnostic and therapeutic purpose)
- Diuretic urine catheter
- Intubation if necessary
- Monitoring of BP, HR, EKG, temp., laboratory tests
Non-variceal→ Pharmacological treatment (prior endoscopy)
- PPI
- Somatostatin → inhibition of gastric/ pancreatic acid secretion
→ Endoscopic treatment (emergency within first 24h)
- Endoscopic injection of vasoconstrictor (alcohol, adrenalin, collagen)
- Plasma coagulation
- Electrocoagulation
- Application of clips
→ Surgical treatment
Indications
1. Massive HDS with vital risk that Ø respond to resuscitation therapy
2. Repeat bleeding in first hours/days after endoscopic hemostasis
3. Lack of response to conservative therapy (endoscopic, medication)
4. Prolonged bleeding with loss > 2 liters of blood
UlcerI. Chronic gastric ulcer or NSAID induced ulcer
- Drug therapy → PPI or H2 receptor inhibitors, protectors of gastric mucosa and
antibiotic anti-Helicobacter pylori
- First endoscopic attempt by adrenalin injection
- If bleeding does not stop, subtotal gastric resection or total gastrectomy
II. Chronic duodenal ulcer
- s. gastric ulcer
- If hemorrhage does not stop, X-suture in situ hemostasis is preferred or Billroth I or
Billroth II gastric resection
Hemorrhagic gastritis- Secondary to NSAID´s: stop drugs, administer PPI or H2 blockers, protectors of gastric
mucosa (eg. sucralfate)
- Anti-Helicobacter pylori antibiotics
- If bleeding does not stop → subtotal gastric resection or total gastrectomy
Gastric CA- First endoscopic hemostasis
- If bleeding continues → subtotal gastrectomy or total gastrectomy
- In unresectable cases → gastric devascularization
- Selective embolization or selective injection of vasoactive substances by
interventional radiologist
Hemobilia- Embolized by interventional radiology
- In case of failure → ligation of hepatic artery (branch corresponding to lesion) or
resection of affected liver segment
Variceal bleeding- Endoscopic treatment: intra- or peri-variceal sclerotherapy, ligation with elastic
bands, hemo clips
- Pharmacological treatment: intraarterial injection of vasopressin, somatostatin,
propranolol (beta-blockers)
- If bleeding continues → Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota balloon tamponade
- If balloon tamponade does not work → transjugular porto-systemic shunt (TIPSS) as
emergency intervention until surgery; candidate for liver transplantation
- If not candidate for liver transplantation → porto-caval shunt, esophageal
transsection (Tanner or Sugiura-Futagawa procedures)

Diagnosis and treatment algorithm

Lower GI bleeding

= loss of blood in digestive tract between Treitz angle and anus

  • Melena
  • Hematochezia
  • Rectorrhagia

Etiology

Small intestine- It is rare, of low intensity, it is externalized by melena
1. Meckel’s diverticulum - common in young people and children
2. Intestinal invagination
3. Crohn's disease
4. Entero-mesenteric infarction
5. Intestinal polyps
Colon1. Colon cancer - one of most common causes, associated with weight loss and
transit disorders
2. Colonic diverticulosis - frequent, stool with fresh blood and mucus
3. Angiodysplasias grow in surface with age, more common in right colon
4. Ulcerative recto-colitis
5. Benign polyp tumors
6. Ischemic and radic colitis
Rectum and perianal region- Relatively frequent, it is externalized through rectorrhagia
1. Hemorrhoids → can cause massive bleedings; hide lower rectal CA
2. Anal fissures
3. Recto-colonic polyposis
4. Rectal trauma
5. Iatrogenic causes

Diagnosis

  • Clinical exam → DRE
  • Lab to detect occult bleeding
  • Imaging → colonoscopy, endorectal US, scintigraphy with marked redness (useful if discontinuous bleeding)
  • Video capsule → radiological exam with contrast/ double contrast for diverticula and tumors

Treatment

  • Endoscopic
  • Surgical

Hematemesis - vomiting of red blood, indicates upper GI bleeding, coffee-ground emesis is vomiting dark brown, granular material that resembles coffee grounds (upper GI bleeding that has slowed or stopped, hemoglobin digested by gastric acid), DD with hemoptysis (foamy blood, no food, after coughing); requires 800-1000 ml of blood

Hematochezia – usually passage of gross, fresh blood from colon (lower GI bleeding) but may result from vigorous upper

GI bleeding with rapid transit of blood through intestines, can be mixed with stool, sometimes clots/ sprinkles on stool, can be also without stools; requires 1000 ml of blood

Melena - black, tarry stool, badly smelling, typically upper GI bleeding but can be from any source in small bowl or right colon, digested by bacteria; requires 50-100 ml of blood

Rectorrhagia – Fresh rectal bleeding, bright red blood on stools, can be without stools

Chronic occult bleeding - anywhere in GI tract, detectable by chemical testing of stool specimen, anemia

book.html:
Upper digestive tract bleedings

Marius Stanca

Upper gastrointestinal bleeding includes all the causes of bleeding of digestive tract from the pharyngo-esophageal junction to the duodeno-jejunal ligament (Treitz).

Classification

The severity of upper gastrointestinal bleeding varies widely from a subclinical bleeding (occult bleeding) manifested as an anemia to major hemorrhage that endanger the patient’s life.

TABLE 1 – Classification of upper gastrointestinal bleeding according

to severity and clinical signs

(HR) are normal (Hb) = 10-12 g/dl

mm Hg

Algover Index (HR/sBP) < 1

pallor, cold sweating, tachypnea

The UDB could be classified in acute and chronic bleeding: acute gastrointestinal bleeding is characterized by blood loss in a short time that can lead to significant hemodynamic disturbances; chronic gastrointestinal bleeding is the loss of small amounts of blood over a long period of time and is manifested by severe anemia, but well tolerated on hemodynamic level.

Etiology

There are multiple causes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding: esophageal diseases: esophageal varices, acute erosive esophagitis, esophageal peptic ulcer, benign esophageal tumor, esophageal cancer, trauma by foreign body, endoscopic exploration and biopsy, instrumental dilatations, Mallory-Weiss syndrome, Boerhaaven syndrome, esophageal diverticula; gastroduodenal diseases: gastric and duodenal ulcer,postoperative peptic ulcer, acute and chronic hemorrhagic gastritis, rare vascular malformation (Dieulafoy’s ulcer), Menetrier's syndrome, hiatal hernia, gastric benign tumors, gastric cancer, gastric mucosal prolapse in the duodenal bulb, gastric and duodenal diverticula, intragastric foreign body, tabetic gastric crisis, gastric syphilis, gastric tuberculosis, aneurysms of the gastric and duodenal arteries, hemorrhagic duodenitis, ampuloma, heterotopic abnormalities (pancreas), Crohn's disease; other gastrointestinal diseases: liver cirrhosis, thrombosis or obstruction of suprahepatic veins ( Budd-Chiari syndrome), choledochal cancer, liver hemangioma, post-traumatic hemobilia, hepatic artery aneurysm, acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis; extradigestive diseases: idiopathic thrombocytopenic thrombotic purpura (Werlhoff disease), hemophilia, Henoch-Schonlein disease, , polycythemia vera, leukemia (especially acute form), Hodgkin's disease, hypoprothrombinemia, hypofibrinogenaemia, fibrinolysis, Glanzmann's thrombasthenia, Willebrand disease, pernicious anemia (Addison-Biermer disease), atherosclerosis, hypertension, dissecting aortic aneurysm, mesenteric and hepatic artery aneurysm, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Rendu disease), generalized telangiectasia, Kaposi syndrome, Gronblad-Strandberg syndrome (hereditary elastodystrophy), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (generalized elastorhexia), mesenteric infarction by thrombosis or embolism, complications after vascular reconstructive surgery (aorto-enteric fistula), periarteritis nodosa, multiple myeloma, digestive sarcoidosis, digestive amyloidosis, uremia; stress status: craniocerebral trauma (Cushing ulcer), brain lesions (Cushing ulcer), intracranial surgery (Cushing ulcer), toxicoseptic shock (Billroth ulcers), extensive burns (Curling ulcer); iatrogenic causes: NSAIDs, steroids, anticoagulants, chemotherapy, reserpine, alcohol.

Clinical aspects

Upper gastrointestinal bleeding is clinically manifested by three main signs: haematemesis (vomiting of red bright blood or clots), melanemesis or vomiting “coffee grounds” (hemoglobin is converted into hydrochloric acid haematin), melena (black stool elimination “as oil”, soft, shiny and bad smelling) and hematochezia (fresh blood from the anus).

Melanemesis occurs when there is low flow of bleeding and there is enough digestion time by hydrochloric acid. When the amount of blood loss is higher (800-1000 ml), the hemorrhage is manifested by haematemesis. Haematemesis have to be differentiated from hemoptysis (elimination of aerated foamy blood, no food leftovers, which appears after coughing). Melena is the most frequent manifestation of UGB and indicates a low flow bleeding and there is enough time to digestion of the blood in the digestive tract. A hemorrhage of 50 ml of blood is required to pass 8-12 hours in the digestive tract for melena. Melena may occur in the lower digestive bleeding, but if it is accompanied by hematemesis, is always a sign of UGB. When there is a high flow bleeding hematochezia appears (when blood loss is more than 1000 ml).

There are occult gastrointestinal bleedings with very little but repeated blood loss, which can sometimes lead to significant anemia, which alarms the patient and this is the starting point of investigations in order to clarify their etiology.

Medical history may reveal a history of peptic ulcer disease, chronic hepatitis / cirrhosis, chronic use of NSAIDs, anticoagulants or blood disorders treatments. Physical examination reveals pallor, fatigue, tendency to fainting. If there is an important bleeding, signs and symptoms may reveal hypovolemia manifested by thirst, restlessness, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension with fainting, asthenia, tachycardia, tachypnea, weak pulse, dyspnea, peripheral hypoperfusion with cold extremities, cold sweats, low blood pressure to collapse and coma. Digital rectal exam confirms melena or hematochezia.

Investigations

For accurate assessment of blood loss and bleeding effect on vital organs, a series of investigations will be performed at admission and in some cases will be repeated at regular intervals (daily or several times a day) to catch a possible recurrence of bleeding.

Emergency investigations include: blood pressure (BP), heart rate (HR) ideally monitored by ECG, blood counts, coagulation and Rh blood group and emergency investigation of upper digestive tract by upper endoscopy (which normally need to explore the upper digestive tract down to the duodenojejunal angle of Treitz and tempt hemostasis in most cases). A series of investigations explore the liver and kidney and for more accurate indication of the etiology some other imaging examinations will be necessary: barium swallow, selective angiography (with the possibility of embolization), scintigraphy with labeled red blood cells, spleno-portography.

Other explorations will investigate the etiology of bleeding, which can be performed after patient stabilization.

Paraclinic diagnosis of occult bleeding test is done by type Gregersen, Hemocult, etc.

Positive and differential diagnosis

Diagnosis of upper gastrointestinal bleeding must be done as quickly as possible to establish the therapeutic protocol. The patient's life depends largely on the rapid ceasing of bleeding and the efficacy of therapeutic measures.

Differential diagnosis of haematemesis is made with haemoptysis (blood is fresh, airy, sparkling, which accompanies the cough), swallowed epistaxis, gums bleeding and nosebleeds and for the melena, with the ingestion of drugs (iron, bismuth, charcoal), lower gastrointestinal bleeding.

Therapeutic Plan

UGB therapy is started the first doctor that examines the patient and may require the expertise of several types of specialties depending on the cause and therapeutic solutions: gastroenterology, endoscopy, surgery, intensive care. The main objectives of the physician are to establish its source and stop the bleeding and stabilize the patient's hemodynamics. The first maneuvers that every doctor must perform in front of UGB are:

  • Installation of 1 or 2 venous access;
  • Taking blood cells counts, coagulation, biochemical tests (electrolytes, urea, creatinine, liver tests, etc.)
  • Blood group and Rh;
  • Administration of crystalloids and whole blood or packed red blood cells (in high UGB)
  • Administration of oxygen

If the patient is hemodynamically stable complement history, focusing on the pathology questions that can evolve with UGB and the medication administered (NSAIDs, corticosteroids, anticoagulants, etc.). Once the physical examination is performed, the nasal-gastric probe is mounted if active bleeding is suspected (except with cirrhosis and esophageal varices known) and emergency upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is performed if active bleeding is suspected.

If the patient is hemodynamically unstable, hemodynamics rebalancing is performed with crystalloids (Ringer's solution and saline) and blood izogrup izoRh. Also a urinary catheter is inserted for diuresis monitoring. Coagulopathy is corrected in cases where it is found coagulation disorders or thrombocytopenia. If the patient is hemodynamically stabilized upper digestive endoscopy is performed but if it remains unstable in the intensive care properly conducted, emergency surgery is indicated.

Active UGB treatment regarding specific causes:

1. Chronic gastric ulcer: are tempted to stop bleeding by endoscopic injection of 0.5-1 ml of adrenaline 0.01 ‰. If successful drug therapy is continued with proton pump inhibitors (eg. omeprazole, lansoprazole) or histamine H2 receptor inhibitors (eg. famotidine, ranitidine, nizatidine), protectors of the gastric mucosa (eg. sucralfate) and antibiotic antiHelicobacter pylori (if indicated). If bleeding does not stop, gastric resection (marginal, 2/3 - Pean (Billroth I), Billroth II gastrectomy or total) - preferably

  • or hemostasis in situ with stitches (depending on the case) is performed.

2. Chronic duodenal ulcer: is tempted to stop bleeding by endoscopic injection of 0.5-1 ml of adrenaline 0.01 ‰. If successful drug therapy is continued with proton pump inhibitors (eg. omeprazole, lansoprazole) or histamine H2 receptor inhibitors (eg. famotidine, ranitidine, nizatidine) and anti-Helicobacter pylori antibiotics (if indicated). If bleeding does not stop the practice of hemostasis in situ with stitches - preferred - or gastric resection 2 / 3 type Pean (Billroth I) or Billroth II.

3. Gastric and esophageal varices: is tempted to stop bleeding by intra- or perivariceal endoscopic sclerotherapy or ligation with elastic bands. Also somatostatin therapy is recommended. If the bleeding continues,a Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota balloon tamponade is recommended. If after balloon tamponade bleeding does not stop there are two alternatives: if the patient is a candidate for liver transplantation a transjugular portosystemic shunt (TIPSS) is performed emergency, as temporary treatment until surgery; if the patient is a not candidate for liver transplantation, a porto-caval shunt (calibrated with synthetic prosthesis or distal spleno- renal Warren), Tanner or Sugiura-Futagawa procedures are performed. For gastric varices endoscopic sclerotherapy is less useful and instead esophageal transsection (Tanner procedure) the surgeon will opt for surgical ligation of varicose veins. If bleeding stops after endoscopy, drug therapy will be continued with betablockers such as propranolol and endoscopic therapy of varices scheduled.

4. Mallory-Weiss syndrome: usually stops spontaneously, but if the bleeding continues endoscopic hemostasis is tempted. If bleeding continues after endoscopic therapy the surgeon will practice suture hemostasis through gastrotomy.

5. Gastric neoplasms: endoscopic hemostasis is tempted. If bleeding continues subtotal gastric resection (4/5) or total gastrectomy is performed. In cases of non-resecable gastric tumors, vascular pedicle ligatures are practiced. Centers with interventional radiology equipment can practice selective hemostasis by embolization or selective injection of vasoactive substances.

6. Acute hemorrhagic gastritis secondary non-steroidal antiinflammatory: stop NSAIDs, administer proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers, protectors of the gastric mucosa (eg. sucralfate) and antiHelicobacter pylori antibiotics (if indicated). If bleeding does not stop the subtotal gastric resection or total gastrectomy is recommended.

7. Hemobilie: embolization by interventional radiology is tempted. In case of failure the ligation of the corresponding hepatic artery branch to the affected lobe is performed or liver resection of the affected segment.

Prophylaxis UGB Prophylaxis is achieved by effective treatment of gastroduodenal ulcers with Helicobacter pylori eradication and systematic administration of proton pump inhibitors, endoscopic treatment of esophageal varices before their rupture and, in tumors, through early detection by screening methods in groups risk patients and their radical treatment.
